utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Paul Rogers appearing on behalf of the Prosecution, together with Ms. Priya Gopalan and our case manager today, Ms. Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Ben Emmerson, Your Honours, for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Mr. Rod Dixon, Ms. Annie O'Reilly, and Mr. Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Emmerson. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Gregor Guy-Smith, good morning, Your Honours, along with Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, and Gentian Zyberi continues to be with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. For Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Richard Harvey for Mr. Brahimaj, with Mr. Paul Troop, Ms. Sophie Rigney, Mr. Luke Boenisch, and again assisted by Ms. Rudina Jasini. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we call Shefqet Kabashi, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I be heard, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it, my client is coming with -- he was coming in with handcuffs. I was going to make sure that those handcuffs were removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, Mr. Kabashi. Good morning to you. Sorry, Mr. Kabashi, we are in court. Can you please face the front and don't communicate with the people in the gallery. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kabashi. I see that you have your counsel present here with you this morning. Is that something you would wish to remain, that Mr. Karnavas stays with you during the course of these proceedings this morning?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, he may stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kabashi, could you give your full names to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Shefqet Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: July the 1st, 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And your place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Zahaq, Peje, the Republic of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your ethnicity, if I may ask that question, please?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I think you know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I know it, but the Court needs to hear it from you. It's the process we have, Mr. Kabashi. I have to ask you questions that don't tell you what the answer is and the Court can then hear it. So I do my best. It may seem strange, and I wonder if you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: May the Honours ask that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: May I lead, please, on this? Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've already indicated to Mr. Rogers that given the particular history of this witness I'm not happy to consent to any leading questions on any subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Even on a simple question of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On any subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. Perhaps Your Honour would be kind enough to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are leading your witness. The Chamber will ask questions when it -- the Chamber is not going to be directed by a witness or not on what procedure to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, are you Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I am Albanian, but I have no reason to answer your questions and you know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kabashi, I want to ask you some questions, please, about what happened in Kosovo in the municipalities of Peje and in the surrounding municipalities in 1998. Now, in the early part of 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: In the early part of 1998, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: What time-period exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, let me start with, let's say, March 1998. Where were you in March 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: At home, in Zahaq.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And did you stay in Zahaq in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Partly. Where else did you go in April 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: May I know why you deem it so significant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are here to answer the questions that the Prosecutor asks you. It's not for you to ask him questions. If you want to ask him questions, wait until we take a break and you can discuss with him outside court. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sure Your Honour didn't intend to indicate that the witness could discuss anything with prosecuting counsel outside of court. It may be that I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When he finishes testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, at the end of his evidence at a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I asked you whether you stayed in Zahaq in April 1998, where else did you go in April 1998? Could you kindly answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I went to join the Kosova Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I ask, please, where it was that you went to join the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: At Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And do you know the municipality in which Jabllanice is?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: It belongs to the municipality of Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And are you able to help, please, with any other villages that are near to it so that we can orientate ourselves a little bit before I show you a map.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Your Honours, may the gentleman on the right ask no further questions because I've got no answers to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Could the map e-court reference 03076 be -- please be put on to the screen. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you can -- I can -- I hope you can see on a screen a map that's rather small, but if we could just enlarge it, as is happening here, you can see the town of Peje -- well, it's marked here as Pec, but using the Albanian name Peje, you can see Peje there - that's enough of the enlargement, thank you - you can see Peje. And then if we can just scroll the screen to the right and to show where Kline is, please. You see there the town of Kline. You see that there, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I wasn't very good at school. I cannot read maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Ah-ha. Can you read the name "Klina"?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I can't see where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I don't know if there's a method whereby I can try to point it out or we can just enlarge it further. Perhaps we can just enlarge it further. Do you see Klina now, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You don't. Well, I could come and physically point it out to you or we could try to find another way to point it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could scroll the map to the left and see if we can find your own village, Zahaq. Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you see towards the top of the map along the road which is the red line about a third of the way along a village marked Zahaq. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All right. You told us that you went to the village of Jabllanice. Can you tell us, please, the date when it was that you went to Jabllanice, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think the witness has already answered that question. My note is that he indicated that he went in April 1998 to Jabllanice when he joined the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I asked the date, a more precise question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Can you help us approximately with the date, please.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Can you help, please, with whether it was towards the beginning or the end of the month?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: In the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Did you go with anybody else or did you go on your own?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I went with my uncle's sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us who they were? Or do you have a reason why you don't wish to say who they are?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I went with Bashkim, my cousin, and then Jaha and Bashkimi after he was wounded in Dubrava as a result of the NATO bombing. After that, he was wounded by a hand-grenade thrown by the Serbs in the Dubrava basement and he died after the war as a result of the injuries sustained there. You didn't want to know about that, neither about those who have found their deaths there nor about the other 200 who also died in basements. So how do you expect me to answer when at a time I was at the Dubrava prison, in the same room, in the same wing, as the one where I find myself now. And now that I've been contained to this one, I have exactly the same memories. I'm expecting the NATO planes to come and bomb at any time, but they won't. I don't know what the frame of mind I am in to be able to carry out these things and to think that it is okay. Is there any force on earth to restrain you, to hold you accountable about what you have done? All you do is ask questions, answer -- and say: Answer, answer, answer. Why? Why should I answer? What's the goal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Control your witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, of course. It may be important to try to allow the witness to speak a little as -- in order to move on. I do understand Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he must speak relevantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I entirely understand. I think for Mr. Kabashi this is relevant for him and important for him to say, and it may assist us to move on if he is allowed to say what it is he feels a little and then perhaps we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: But I move -- I'm going back to questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think if -- this is not a criticism in any way, but if Mr. Karnavas is consulting with Mr. Kabashi during his testimony, then I think we ought to perhaps have some understanding of what the parameters of that is now that he's begun his evidence. I'm sorry, I don't mean to intrude upon it, but simply some understanding of what principles the Court is operating upon, if there is consultation taking place during testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would agree. I would suggest that if Mr. Kabashi wishes to speak with Mr. Karnavas, perhaps he could first indicate that to Your Honours, and then Your Honours can determine whether it is appropriate for him to speak with his counsel during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if I might, Your Honour, and I don't know what Mr. Karnavas's intentions are, but I do know having represented a many a witness and many a witness in the setting of federal court and state court in the United States, that there is more of an open flow as between the attorney and the witness. And considering that Mr. Karnavas is not only representing him as a witness in this case but is also representing him with regard to a case in which he has his own personal criminal liability, I believe that he may have some legal understanding, some legal concerns, that we may not be privy to. I don't know. I don't know whether that's the case or not, but I rise because that is one of the functions for counsel I would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may explain. You and Mr. Emmerson and everybody, the money that he got for the Defence of the defendants would have been best spent somewhere in Kosova. There would be no need for about 20 of you to be around the courtroom here. You could have helped the homeless, people who were maimed, who lost their loved ones during the war. I mean the millions that you have received. And there's no need for you to interrupt because I'm fully aware of what I'm saying. I know that I'm innocent. I've done nothing. That's why I asked Their Honours to ask the questions because the Defence and the Prosecution are the same. You're a Defence lawyer today, you're a Prosecutor tomorrow. All you want to do is just earn some more money, but you don't care at all about who was killed where over there, but that is important enough for me. I gave my evidence to KFOR, the Kosova police -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please. Can I -- just one point. When somebody's speaking, we wait for him to finish. We don't interrupt him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking when they interrupted me. If they have a right to interrupt me, do I not have the same right? So that I'm clear, if I don't have that right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He did not interrupt you. We give each other a chance to finish what we are saying, but we try also to speak relevantly to the issues. May I just mention to both you and Mr. Karnavas that when you do want to chat, say -- consult, give an indication to the Bench that you do want to do that and we'll give you that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, can I just take you back, please, you were telling --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, can I just take you back, please, to April 1998 --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [In English] Get to the point what you want to know from me. You don't need to know my life. You don't need to know where I went this time and that time. What you are interested to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: What I know to know is what you saw, if anything, in Jabllanice when you were there as a member of the KLA. So when you first went there, who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About what, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: About when you joined the KLA, who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I spoke to a number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Could you name them?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: If you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: It's a large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All right. Start with the first one you spoke to about your joining the KLA --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I said it's a lot of people and maybe amongst them are people who would prefer to have their names withheld. It's people who are not present here anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Why did you go to Jabllanice to join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I do not know how to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, why did you go there and not anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I went to join the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, why did you go there and not anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Because my family's from there and I was more interested in that particular territory because that's my origin, my family origin. From Zhabel which is the village nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you know the village of Gllogjan, Catholic Gllogjan as I will call it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Is that -- that's also near Jabllanice, that you went to?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know -- I do know, but do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: When you first went there to join, was there anybody that you understood was in charge of that group of the KLA there; and if so, who was that person or persons?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I said earlier, show me what your intention is. What do you want to know in particular? Don't beat about the bush --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because I am a simple person, I am taken aback by things easily. So maybe I will give you a wrong answer. So please tell me what your intention is. I don't want to make a mistake. In fact, I don't know what mistake I have committed to be arrested, to be put in prison. What have I done? What have I done to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, it was a simple question as to who you understood was in charge of the group of the KLA at Jabllanice when you reported there. So I wonder if you could tell us who you understood was in charge at that time, and it may be more than one person.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Will you first tell me why I was imprisoned, why I was detained, why am I sitting side by side with people accused of crimes? I've seen courage playing tennis. I'm going there and sitting side by side with the same people, and then you expect me to testify here before this Court to say something. How can I do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you asked me to get to the point and ask you some direct questions, and I'm trying to do that. And the direct question I asked you was: When you went to Jabllanice, who did you understand was in charge of the KLA group in Jabllanice and it may be more than one person. So would you please answer that simple question.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I have followed the proceedings of this Tribunal and all the questions relate to one thing. Do you want me to speak about the Jabllanice detention centre or prison? Don't beat about the bush. Tell me straight for what you want from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kabashi. Tell us about the Jabllanice detention centre or prison. Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: There was no prison in Jabllanice, and I can swear by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: But it's your phrase, words, "prison, detention centre," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I said do you want to know about the Jabllanice prison? Is that your intent? You have asked me for the umpteenth time and you are asking me for the same thing. I think the investigator has made a mess of it. I can't put some order in this mess created by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Were there people detained at the Jabllanice barracks or place? Were people detained there where the KLA were?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't see any prisoners there. People came in and went out very easily. There was a guard at the gate of the staff. Inside there were no doors, there were no locks. Many rooms didn't have any doors. I did -- I don't know that there was anything forbidden in the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: What was your role there, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I was a soldier. I was maybe one of the few that remained a soldier because the others became commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And what did you do there in Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Many things. What do you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: In particular, at the -- first of all, was there a place where soldiers stayed together? Was there a barracks?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Where was the barracks located?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: In Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Whereabouts in Jabllanice was the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: There were three or four. I don't know which one you want me to answer about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, do you remember when you spoke to investigators that you drew some sketches?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you remember signing those sketches when you were trying to explain about the location?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: From last Thursday to today I have signed some 20 papers. So, to tell you the truth, I don't know what is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: -- they tell me to sign and I sign. It's the same thing that happened to me with the Serbs, they told me, "Sign this because there is no other way," and I was forced to do that. The powerful can force you to do things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at 03015 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply rise at this point because obviously from a procedural point of view this is indistinguishable from putting a witness statement to a witness. The fact that the map that he proposes to put to -- Mr. Rogers proposes to put to the witness is graphic rather than the written word makes no difference because it is part of the witness statement. So if a witness's witness statement is going to be used in chief, Mr. Rogers needs to make an application and lay the foundation for doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I just did lay the foundation for doing it. The foundation was that the witness agreed that he had drawn some sketch maps during the course of his interviews, and I'm showing what we say is one of them. And the witness can comment upon it or not as we go. I think my learned friend knows well I have laid the foundation for this question. So perhaps the witness could please be shown 03 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say yes that I did some sketches. I have drawn these sketches, but I don't know your purpose in asking me these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It will all become clear, Mr. Kabashi, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, if you'll just look at it, first of all, please, and then we'll take it one question at a time. Now, if you would kindly look at the document, 03015.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Is it on the screen? Page 16, I think, in e-court. Forgive me. It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Is that something you drew?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And is it signed at the bottom by you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And has it got words written on it by you?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, perhaps we can look at it.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You can see there at marked E a place that you have called army barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: In point A you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: E, E.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the place that was the barracks, as you've marked, in which people were detained; is that right? First of all, is that the barracks that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, that is the barracks, but there were no detainees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No. Well, I want you to help me, if you would, please, with the building, the square object, rectangular object, that is marked in the centre of the compound. Can you see that, first of all? Do you see it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Which one? There are many --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The rectangular one that is marked --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: -- rectangular facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- in the centre or near the centre of the compound. Not the ones that appear to be attached to walls, but the one that is standing alone within the compound within the marked area. You see that building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, when you say "within the compound," did you mean the place -- the picture marked E?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Within the picture marked E. It was unclear. You see that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see marked in the top left-hand corner of that building the letter H?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you see what you've written at the top of the page "H - Detention Centre." What did you mean by that when you wrote "detention centre"?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't write that word. [In English] I never wrote there. That's not my writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: That's not your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Whose handwriting is that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Probably one of your boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: What do you say, then, about the room that is marked H as detention centre?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not a detention centre. I myself used to sleep in that very room. Several times I have slept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: What was that building used for?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: For the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And what else was it used for?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: To sleep there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Can I show you some photographs, please. First of all, can I show you 65 ter 03054.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can -- could that -- the map actually please be an exhibit? Before I get to the photograph, could I please exhibit there the map that has just been shown and identified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers, the Registrar correctly asks that there was -- states that there was a map and a sketch. What is it that you are tendering into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Sorry, forgive me, the sketch. Just the sketch. The map we didn't get very far with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03015 will be Exhibit P118.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, could you look at this photograph, please. Can you tell me what it shows.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: You mean the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But as a matter of housekeeping, as I understand it that is -- that particular 65 ter number includes the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I only want that one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I think that's just the one page that's been --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well, I just want to double-check that it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm not intending to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If anything else becomes relevant later, we'll deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Of which, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The photograph, 03054.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us, Mr. Kabashi, where this photograph is taken?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You don't. Have you seen it before? Has this photograph been shown to you before, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I've seen many things. I can't remember all. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you remember ever during the course of your interview with investigators that you were shown a series of photographs?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown several photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kabashi, this photograph is identified in your statement as one of those you were shown. Now, I'd ask you to look at it again, please, and help me with whether this is the place that you have described as the barracks or have drawn on the sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that's a -- that question is leading as presently framed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, he's drawn a picture, he's described going to a barracks, and I think he's entitled to say whether this photograph does or does not show that barracks. He may say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question is still leading, Mr. Rogers. A sketch is one thing, a photograph is another. He can tell us what he knows about this photograph without you suggesting to him what the answer should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: What do you suggest -- are you able to help with where this photograph was taken, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I see a burned house here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'll have to try it another way.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: It's not the same that I was in at that time. It's different. That was rather different from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: How was it different?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: If you are asking me whether this is the place that I used to stay, I'm saying that it doesn't seem the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to me the same. It's much different than the one I was in. So I can't say for sure that this is the place. Since it's not the same. Many things there are not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I understand that the -- it may be that the state of the buildings is in a different state to when you remember it. But I'm asking you whether you recognise any part of it as being the place where you stayed.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I told you earlier -- I gave you the answer as much as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: All right. You were shown this photograph together with others when you provided a statement in 2007 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would request that Mr. Rogers refrain from testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Well, I can show the statement. I'm getting to that. It's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think Mr. Rogers is entitled to show the statement. He needs to proceed according to the Rules and on principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yeah, the principle is of memory-refreshing in this Tribunal. The witness has repeatedly stated he is not sure, I can't remember. I want to show him the statement where he refers to these specific photographs, and that seems to me to be admissible, respectfully, course of action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Provided that we have admitted that statement with -- because it has passed the admissibility standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I don't think I need to have the statement admitted, respectfully, for it to be shown as a memory-refreshing document to the witness. Your Honour will recall that if we proceed down a particular route where we may end up with this witness that I have to go through a number of stages. The first of which is to go through a memory-refreshing stage. All right. It's 03016. And it's paragraph 29 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we go to that 03016, what are you doing with 03054?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just taking it off the screen for the moment. The witness hasn't identified it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It's the same paragraph reference in the Albanian statement as well. It's paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: First of all, before we move on, do you see your signatures on the bottom of each of the page? Is that your signature at the bottom there, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I said earlier yes, it is, and I said that ever since I came here last Thursday I have given 20 or some signatures. They've told me, "Sign it," and I've signed it. I know what this is about. I've read it several times, but there are many untrue things in this sentence -- in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Let me just ask -- can I --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: But I think the investigator has made many mistakes, mistakes which has even cost human lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, just look at paragraph 29 of this statement that you have signed both in Albanian and in English. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Just read it to yourself. When you've read it, tell me. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: What do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Have you read the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you. You see there a series of photograph numbers referred to there and you said, paragraph 29, in the second line -- third line: "I have seen some photographs of the barracks. These are identified by ERN numbers U0184-3082 [sic] ..." plus others. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The photograph that I have just shown you, e-court number 03054, is the first of those listed photographs that you have described as the barracks. Now, does that help your memory?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: To remember what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: This is a photograph showing the barracks that you reported to in Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I told you even earlier what was discussed with the investigators and then what happened afterwards for me to sign it. It's not the same stuff. This has been elaborated, changed. I told you that I have signed many things. I may sign a document that I killed Barack Obama, but now nobody has killed him. I told you earlier when I came out of that war, when I came out of the prison in Dubrava, the Serbian prison, for me it was the same, it amounted to the same thing. And I have no regrets that your investigators are even worse than the ones of the Serbs. They beat you up, but these ones here drain your blood slowly and this is what happened not with me alone. They are asking me whether I am afraid or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: It's not a question of being afraid, Mr. Rogers. You have to come to the point. I'm trying to go to the crux of the problem, where the problem lies. With your investigators, with your work, you are trying to make me speak about something which is not at all important regarding in the context of the war crimes committed there in Yugoslavia. If you are talking and if we are discussing about the crimes committed in Yugoslavia for which this Tribunal was set up, you've done nothing. In fact, you have done more -- committed more crimes with your deeds and everyone knows that. If I am talking here -- if I am saying here something that -- for which tomorrow you can accuse me, you can increase the number of charges brought against me, you can put me in jail, but it won't change my conviction what I know and what all the world knows, what is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Would you please allow me to ask my next question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I won't allow you to ask questions of me because what I've been through, I don't know how I have put up with being here. I don't know how I am taking all of this and I am warning even the distinguished honours coming from very different countries, I don't know who they are, but please leave me in peace. If you send me to prison, then don't ask me any questions. I might lose my mind, I might lose control of myself, and then you can send me to jail again. If you want me to speak dirty words, bad words, then I will do that; but if you want to allow me to testify as a normal human being, as God has made me, please allow. Don't push me too much. You have to acknowledge your mistakes. I don't know who is going to try you. I don't know if there is anyone that can try you. Since you are trying me for what? And putting me in jail? And then you who have done so many crimes, nobody is judging you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Is this Tribunal set up for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's clearly not going to be possible to try to continue to answer questions at this precise moment in time. I would ask and invite Your Honours to adjourn briefly to allow the witness to recompose himself and then he can come back. Because I've tried several times now to interject to control this, and I can't because the witness won't stop now. I would suggest we take a short break or if Mr. Kabashi is sufficiently composed to deal with the next question, then I will deal with the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long do you want to take a break for?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Kabashi is prepared to answer the next question of him without ranting --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can ask you one further thing because you are interrupting me continually. Permit me to ask a single question, please. You're asking me about what happened at Jabllanice, how many people were killed, how many were killed, five, six, ten? Why did you never, you, yourself, of your workers, why did you never ask us about the 200 people who were killed, who were massacred, in the course of two or three days? Who is the one who testified before The Hague Tribunal on the 200 killed at Dubrava, of the people killed in the basement where I was present, of the ones who were stabbed after being killed. And I was hiding myself in the boilers in that basement but nobody is asking me to give any evidence of that because somebody else has said -- the others who were with me, however, my uncle's sons and the others, and I can give names, if you want, and none of them have been asked to come here to give evidence. I can state here that there is no justice at all. Don't ask me to answer questions. This is rubbish. What you're dealing with is absolutely rubbish. This money could have been sent to Hollywood to make a good movie for the whole world to understand what had occurred. But everybody has lost their belief in justice because of you in Kosova and in Bosnia, the two countries that suffered the greatest losses in the course of the war. And you are mentioning here three or four people who have been killed there. I'm not defending those ones who have been committed, whoever has committed a crime has to be held accountable, but there is no justice as I can see. Take me into prison and keep me there if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I'm going to take you back to the paragraph I just showed you relating to the photographs, and in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do that, have you abandoned your request for a short break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just trying to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you stated in that statement that you made signed in --

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't say anything. It's not true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... can we give Mr. Rogers a chance to finish his question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he hasn't finished. Mr. Kabashi, you stated that -- in that statement that you made and then you interrupted him. What is the question? You interrupted him. Look at the script -- the transcript, his statement is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The question was that in the statement you were referred you've said: "I have drawn a rough sketch of the location of different buildings including the KLA HQ and the KLA barracks where people were detained in Jablanica." I want to ask you: Were people detained in Jabllanice as you've described in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I didn't say that and I know nothing about it. You are the ones who ought to know, you are the ones who ought to have investigated, who ought to have worked. You didn't do your job and I have no idea why you are pursuing it further and I plead with the honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, do you know a man called Pal Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And do you know a man called Skender Kuci?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I know him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And whilst you were in Jabllanice, did you ever see either of those men in Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No. Skender Kuci used to be one of my neighbours, Pal used to work at Kline, he had a burger shop or a kebab shop. As a young man I used to go out with his younger brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see them whilst you were at Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You didn't?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Never once?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many times do I have to answer the same question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you testified under oath in this Tribunal in the Limaj case and you testified about these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, if Mr. Rogers is starting to cross-examine his own witness, we need to move into a different phase of this proceeding, and he needs to be in a position to lay a foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm trying to lay the foundations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Is it right that you testified in the Limaj case?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Is it right that you testified about both of these --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, another problem, and for this we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's at my request, Your Honour, that you've come in without Mr. Kabashi, and I would ask that we go into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Are there any further submissions the parties would like to make in open session before we call the witness in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, might I just have ten minutes to check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- some material. Yes, and then I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break for ten minutes and come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 11.16 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much for that time. We've been able to identify what I needed to identify, and I'm content that the publicly available records reflect that which was submitted by the Prosecution, as I anticipated it would, but I -- without seeing the actual references, I couldn't check them myself, but there are a few and I have and I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: May the witness be re-called back into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: In fact, whilst the witness is being called, I just need to make a small alteration to the transcript, if I may. At page 41, line 5, I inadvertently referred to the two individuals we may end up speaking about as witnesses. They're not witnesses, they're victims. Perhaps the transcript reference could be corrected to show it as victims, not witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And may I just say to you, Mr. Kabashi, I'm sure you would like to go home as soon as you possibly can. I will ask you to please listen carefully to the questions from Mr. Rogers, the Prosecutor, and try to stay focused on the question and answer just that question that he's asking you. That way, we will finish quicker and you will be free to go home earlier than otherwise would be the case. And I'm sure his questions will be fairly straightforward. If you know, you know; if you don't know, you don't know. May I just mention also perhaps something we should have mentioned to you in the beginning, that if there is any question that you feel uncomfortable answering and you feel it might incriminate you, say to him: I wish not to answer that question. But don't go into a long explanation why you don't want to answer that question, just very short answers. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, before the break I was asking you about whether you knew two men, Pal Krasniqi and Skender Kuci. And I was asking if you had seen them at Jabllanice. I want to clarify your answer and make sure I understand what you are saying now. Did you ever see either of those two men at the Jabllanice barracks in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Why can't you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Did you see them or was it that you don't wish to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: It's not that I don't wish, but I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Can you remember the events in 1998 at the barracks at Jabllanice involving these men?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No. Well, I wonder if you could have a look at your statement, please. It's 0301 -- 3016 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- might, Your Honour. The manner in which this question is going on I think is a bit curious, strange. The gentleman's asked twice whether he can answer a question, he responds that he cannot. Thereafter, he's asked a slightly different question and then Mr. Rogers is going to attempt to refresh his recollection, something that he's done before. And I think at some point in time there has to be a determination of whether or not the witness can or cannot answer a question. If he wishes to refresh recollection, that's quite distinct from the issue of whether he can or cannot answer a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You started off by saying the manner in which this question is asked is curious --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is a bit curious, strange --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you objecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or are you just telling us that it's curious?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm objecting. And I'm objecting on the grounds that the question has been asked and answered now twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, and because it's been asked and answered twice, counsel is trying to refresh the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, no, he said "I can't answer the question." I cannot answer the question. Now, that has some significance, and with regard to what the witness said precisely, he says: "It's not that I don't wish, but I can't." Now, he doesn't inquire any further into why he can't and I think in the absence of getting an answer to that particular question, the manner that this particular questioning is going on is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, yes. Your Honours, in my submission the stage has come where it's proper to put to the witness what he may have said previously in his statements to see whether the reason why he can't answer the question is because he can't remember whether -- or maybe there is some other explanation. I attempted to elicit that, I hope, earlier by asking whether he did not wish to answer the question. But the purpose of showing him the document is to see if he is able to refresh his memory from that. I can ask the witness -- I see Mr. Guy-Smith rises again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, why can you not answer that question?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The question as to whether you saw Pal Krasniqi and Skender Kuci at the Jabllanice barracks in 1998. Why can you not answer that question?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: You were asking something else that has to do with the earlier statement. I thought that was the question you were aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you've told us that you didn't -- that you could not see these or did not see these witnesses at the barracks in 1998. I want to ask you then about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's actually not what he said. He -- you said to him: "Can you remember the events in 1998 at the barracks in Jabllanice involving these men?" And he said: "No, I cannot remember" -- I'm adding "I cannot remember," but his answer was "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me, I thought I asked earlier whether he had seen the men at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You had asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you said, Did you see them or was it that you don't wish -- okay, It's not that I don't wish, but I can't. And you said, Can you remember the events? That's when you then referred to a statement and Mr. Guy-Smith stood up. I was just telling you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the last question before the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you recall making some statements to Prosecutors during the course of 2007 and before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And during the course of those statements, you referred to a number of events, do you remember, at Jabllanice barracks during 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Can you be more specific. Which statement do you mean? There are quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. We can take the most recent one, the 10th, 12th, 14th of May, 2007, which is a consolidated statement relating to the events that you described. That's the most recent one. That's some while ago now, but it is the most recent. It's 65 ter number 3016. Do you recall providing that statement?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: This statement was taken a little -- a few moments or a few -- a little time before I was asked to come and give evidence here, and I asked for changes to be made to the 2004, they weren't, i.e., there's been a mix-up with the 2004 statement which you refused to change and which your investigator, H arjit Sandhu, gave me a leaflet that said: If you do not answer the questions and a number of laws, which I'm not familiar with, I incurred the possibility of a seven-year sentence. At the time I was not ready to submit to a new jail sentence. I had just emerged from prison and he has done whatever he wanted with my statement. So what I said in my evidence at the Limaj case and what I'm saying today, yes, I accept that but for -- on a number of occasions now I've said that whatever you see in those statements is not true. In a manner of speaking, I was forced to sign them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kabashi, I note that you are referring to a statement of 2004. The Prosecutor was asking you about the statement of 2007, which is the most recent one. So I don't know whether any mistakes that you say were made in the 2004 statement were -- whether they were resolved in the 2007 statement, but could you stay with the 2007 statement rather than the 2004 statement because that's what he's asking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was referring to, the amendments were not made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- interprets you as referring to the 2004 statement, but counsel was asking you about the 2007 statement. You may proceed, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you, I note from your evidence, that you referred to saying: "What I said in my evidence at the Limaj case and what I'm saying today ... I accept that but for -- on a number of occasions now I've said that whatever you see in those statements is not true." Do you stand by what you said in the Limaj trial when you testified before the Court then?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, on my evidence there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: What you said to that Trial Chamber was the truth, was it, Mr. Kabashi?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes, on my evidence before the court of law, yes, from what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you recall speaking to that Trial Chamber about the events relating to Pal Krasniqi and Skender Kuci?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Would you like me to show the transcript to you where you spoke about those events so that you can refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Okay. It's 65 ter 3047 and it starts at page 81. Do we have it? And you will see in here a reference to a question at the top of the page -- I'll come back to the times in a moment, but do you see at the top of the page there, there is a question. Are you able to read this in English, Mr. Kabashi, or would you wish it to be translated? Are you able to read it in English? Mr. Kabashi, are you able to read it in English?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [In English] I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could go through it together. It says at the top: "Q. Witness, was there somebody else at that barracks at some point that was detained, someone that you knew from before?" And you answered: "Yes." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought the purpose of this exercise was to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question just asked certainly doesn't do that. If the witness is given an opportunity to read, then he can answer Mr. Rogers' question, which is: After having reviewed the document whether it does refresh or doesn't refresh his memory with regard to those events, by that I mean the event of testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm content for the witness to read through. I was not certain that he was understanding it because it's not in his own language, hence I was reading it out, to see whether he agreed with each portion of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I guess Mr. Kabashi said he was reading it, but let's give him a chance to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to read the entire transcript, Mr. Kabashi, it's just those few questions at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You refer there to Pal Krasniqi and Skender Kuci; correct?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And you -- do you recall now, having refreshed your memory, about when it was that you saw them at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: You've just read the beginning part of that transcript that refers to a time-frame. Having refreshed your memory from it, have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, the question remains the same, and the purpose of refreshing memory is you give somebody a document or some other piece of evidence and they are able to examine it. After that the question remains the same: Is your memory refreshed or not? If the witness indicates his memory is not refreshed, you can't say "your memory is refreshed," that's improper because the exercise here is specifically limited to the issue of refreshing memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just simply gives the witness an opportunity to clarify with the Court, if he wishes, whether he does or does not remember his mind having been directed more specifically to the actual thing that it is alleged he said, bearing in mind the witness's answer already is that everything he said in the Limaj trial was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, he did not, with respect, say everything he said in the Limaj trial was true. I was careful at that stage to watch the way the question and answer was delivered. Because clearly if Mr. Rogers wants to elicit testimony through memory-refreshing, he's going to need to do what he's doing now which is to go through the testimony, invite the witness to refresh his memory and ask him now whether he recalls it, and that's obviously going to be a point-by-point analysis of the testimony he gave in Limaj. He gave a large amount of testimony in Limaj across a very broad range of issues, most of which had nothing to do with Jabllanice, as Mr. Rogers has carefully emphasised to Your Honours already. We don't know what it is precisely the witness was referring to in the answer that he gave. And it certainly can't be taken as a categoric adoption of each and everything that appears on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be heard because now Mr. Emmerson is insinuating, perhaps it was a mistake, but he is insinuating that my client committed perjury in the Limaj case, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If he would just sit down and wait his turn. I lack the civility that Mr. Rogers has, and I will attack when my client is attacked. Now, he was posed a question. If we go back to the record - and that's something that the Prosecution should have done but did not do - in the Limaj case he's asked specifically on page 4179 if he gave a statement and if it was voluntary and if he was truthful. And he said -- and it's over here: "And apart from some corrections and explanations which we have discussed earlier this week, were you as truthful as you could be in those statements?" Meaning 2004, October and December. And the answer is: "Yes." He then testifies and he answers all the questions. Now, if Mr. Emmerson or someone else thinks that he perjured himself in that testimony then they should point out where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm absolutely not suggesting anything of the sort. I'm simply say that if Mr. Rogers wishes to use the transcript as memory refreshing, then he needs to direct the witness's attention to which parts of the transcript he's referring to. I'm making no such suggestion against Mr. Kabashi or any either suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, this whole dilemma started because of the following question and answer. The question posed by Mr. Rogers at page 56, line 2, was: "And do you recall now, having refreshed your memory, about when it was that you saw them at the barracks?" And his answer is: "I can't remember." So obviously his memory is not refreshed as a result of reading that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose you are going to have to take --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And make sure that your questions follow logically --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- on the previous question. The purpose was to refresh your memory. Then let's find out whether the memory has been refreshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, we'll need to go line by line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Page 81 of the e-court transcript, 4225 the actual transcript -- that's why I was attempting to go line by line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If you look, please, Mr. Kabashi at what is line 5. You see the question and answer: "Were there people that you knew from beforehand?" And you gave an answer. Having looked at the answer between lines 5 and 7, is your memory now refreshed as to the time and the number of persons that you saw?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, all right.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Read on a little bit, please, from lines 8 down to line 12 and you'll see a reference there to the two men that we've been speaking about. Is your memory refreshed now as to those two men and whether you saw them?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: What are you aiming at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: His aim is unimportant, Mr. Kabashi. Just the question is: Is your memory refreshed after having read those lines? I know you answered it, but he's asking you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rogers could have had a deeper investigation about what he's referring to. He certainly had all the capabilities. He's too late now to speak about these things, in my view. He is meaningless to continue to talk about these things now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, well it may -- you might think it is meaningless, but it is not for purposes of what we are here about. And what Mr. Prosecutor wants to find out from you is just whether your memory has been refreshed after having read lines 5 to 7 on the transcript of your testimony in the Limaj case. And I think the answer to that question is very simply: Yes, my memory is refreshed; or no, my memory is not refreshed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you started to speak, Your Honour, you said the aim is what happened, the aim which has not been apparent to me on the part of the Prosecution so far. Had the Prosecution had that aim, it would have gone to -- out of its way to make everything possible, to realise it. I come from that country, I have been there. They haven't done even 1 per cent of the work. That is why I am unable to say or to speak about things which are not considered by justice because there is no justice here. I don't think that the justice is brought here before you, Your Honours. There are many, many other things that have been disregarded, have not been investigated to come to justice, to come to the phase where we know what has everyone done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now can I stop you, Mr. -- look, I'm going to stop you. We -- I don't know how deep the Prosecution should or should not have gone. That is really not material for purposes of this exercise. The question that is being put to you is a very simple one: Whether your memory has been refreshed after reading what you see in lines 5 to 7 of your testimony in the Limaj trial. And if you will just say whether your memory is refreshed or not refreshed, we will then move a little further on with this and you will probably go home a little bit sooner than you probably might if you don't answer. I don't think it's for you or I to comment on how the Prosecution investigated this case, whether deep or not deep. Just answer the question and then we will go home sooner, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible to know why I cannot know why the Prosecution didn't conduct its investigation properly? Why when I belonged to that country, to that place. Can you please explain to me why I don't have this right. If you do, I will be very frank and try to do my best to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why I am that collaborator that was sought by the Prosecution, to co-operate with it, to discover the crimes perpetrated? So if you don't perform your duty well, like the Prosecution has, then why should I be under an obligation to answer questions posed to me by the Prosecution? Where is the crux of the matter? Why should I feel obligated to answer it? And they were not obligated to go to the root of the crime, to know who the perpetrators were or in the case of Skender Kuci. There are rumours that he was taken from the place he was working. He was there with other people. The entire village, my village, and other villages know who took him, where they took him, and what happened. Why the Prosecution can't know this, why the Prosecution should ask me when the Prosecution had the necessary data to go to the person who knows who took him. Why have they been discriminating me vis-a-vis other witnesses. They haven't taken the witnesses who should come here to testify, they haven't. They have had a lot of data on crimes committed. Your Honour, in my opinion, if we want to do justice to the victims, we should find who committed the crime, who committed the offence, and find the witnesses. They haven't done that and I can produce facts to prove my point. I don't like to mention names, I don't want to do harm to anyone or to do an honour, if that's the case. I said in 2007, even before, I was not willing to go back to jail because I have a family to keep. I want to express my gratitude to my brother and others that helped me. People who have been working 15- 16-day hour days to keep their families and help me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, sorry. I must ask you once again to please stay short and just to answer the questions from the Prosecution. We are trying to do here just what you say should be done. You are being asked to help to tell us what you know about this case, and if you know something, tell us; if you don't know, you don't know. Just answer the questions of the Prosecutor. I think the Prosecutor has done his job the best way he thinks he should do it. And you and I -- I don't know what you mean by "he's not doing his job well," because I don't know whether you know what his job is. But just answer his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may heard, Mr. President, just very briefly. There is a sense of frustration on the part of Mr. Kabashi because he came forward when nobody else would or did back right after he was released from prison, where he was tortured effectively for three years. He gave information to the authorities in Kosovo, the local authorities, the United Nations, and the ICTY. Those authorities did zero. They did nothing. He came to the Limaj case, it was poorly prosecuted. In his opinion other evidence was not investigated, and so he felt and he feels today a sense of betrayal. He's now being asked to come here today and testify again. He does not believe that the Prosecution has ever been serious in this case, and that's why there is a sense of frustration on his part. And he wanted to make this known to the Trial Chamber. And hopefully now that he has made this known, he may be able to answer some questions so that you can go on about your business and he can go on about his business. But I must say, I must say, and I say this regrettably, that coming here as a witness and being handcuffed at the airport and then taken to the UNDU like a prisoner and then being woken up every 30 minutes where they check you at night, every 30 minutes, reminds him of what it was like when he was in prison and he was being woken up every 30 minutes to get a beating. And that's what we're dealing with here today and it's regrettable. But I understand his sense of frustration, and I certainly see Your Honours are being very, very patient. But I think now that he's finished at least explaining why he feels betrayed and that there is no sense of justice overall, hopefully we can go about the business of answering some questions so we can get out of here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
