utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, just one thing in terms of Mr. Karnavas's testimony, which is with regard -- with regard to the issue of beating, since there's been the issues of Mr. Kabashi being beaten, it's my understanding - and perhaps this -- I could be corrected - it's my understanding that he was beaten by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's while he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to, the three years that he spent as a prisoner of war why the Serbs. And so now he's back up and, you know, every 30 minutes they're checking up. There is such a thing called post-traumatic stress disorder, and I believe we may be dealing with -- I'm not a specialist, but I've dealt with the issue long enough to know we're dealing with a situation where the Court, the Trial Chamber -- the Judge who ordered his arrest and, of course, now him being here handcuffed, I'm unable to see him, all of these are playing into this situation and it's regrettable. But he's doing his level best under the circumstance. I know it doesn't seem that way, but he is doing his level best to co-operate, and hopefully now he'll be able to answer the questions, but we do need to go step by step. And it would be, far be it for me to give advice -- some foundations occasionally might help so we don't get the sort of objections that we are getting which, in my opinion, in many instances are proper objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Karnavas. I hope as you right -- as you say, that now that he has -- Mr. Kabashi has expressed his feelings we might be able to move a little forward with the case. Mr. Kabashi, I ask you now that we have heard your frustrations, your counsel has explained them -- elaborated on them, I hope that we can now -- you are now in a better position to answer the questions of the Prosecutor. Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, I return to these two men, Pal Krasniqi and Skender Kuci. What can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, about what you saw or heard in relation to those men in Jabllanice in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I see we are going back to square one. If it's possible, just I would like to give a brief example to you, Your Honours. If a witness testifies, provides data, on a crime committed and at the same time he knows, he recognises, the person who has committed the crime, that is the perpetrator, he provides the Prosecution with that data. The perpetrator is today free, was never, never detained, never charged - and I am speaking specifically of the same subject matter, as I have seen many things in my life - how can I trust that Prosecution that it has done the best thing? This is just a simple example. Please, Your Honours, tell me, how can I trust such a Prosecution? This was a simple example to make you understand my position and the work done by the Prosecution and its investigators. If you convince me or explain to me why this is the case. Earlier on, Your Honour, you told me that it's not up to me or to you to judge the work of the Prosecution. Maybe it's not, but for me it is because I come from that country and I know very well, and many other witnesses know very well, what they have done, witnesses who have been either disappeared or don't -- or refuse to come here. I know very well who the witnesses should be -- should have been. Where are those witnesses? So you expect me to give names about witnesses, then other conflicts may ensue. I think -- let the Prosecution tell me where are the suitable or adequate witnesses who should have come here to testify? And I know that they know very well what I'm talking about. I'm not the witness that should have taken the stand here. I should have come here after all the other people who should have come here to testify should have come here. Those witnesses who have been eye-witnesses are no longer alive, either they have been killed or disappeared. And I know that the Prosecution has questioned such witnesses. I'm not talking of one single witnesses, but of several such witnesses. Let the Prosecution tell me, where are these witnesses that the Prosecution has questioned? I was lucky that I am still alive. Where is the destiny of those other witnesses that are no longer here? Even on television I have heard that witnesses have been intimidated, they are afraid, both by the -- such words have been mentioned by the Prosecution and by the Defence as well. But I'm talking -- I'm saying the truth here. Let them tell me where are those witnesses. I know very well that they were witnesses and today they are no longer alive. Let the Prosecution tell me who will be responsible for the lost lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may ask you a question, Mr. Kabashi. Does the Chamber understand you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- to be saying you are fearful of testifying here for your life because some witnesses who did testify previously have either been killed or dis -- or they have disappeared? Is that the reason? Is that why you don't want to testify? And you can just say yes or no. You don't have to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not afraid, Your Honour. I'm not afraid. I am afraid of something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about other witnesses. I didn't mean myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. No, no, I understand you. I understand you. You keep saying we must -- the Prosecutor must tell you where those people are, and you seem to know that they have been killed or they disappeared somehow. And I'm asking you: Is that the reason you don't want to testify, because people who testified have either been killed or they have disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not the reason, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any other reason why you don't want to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of the reasons, but there are other reasons that I enumerated earlier, namely, that the witnesses who should have come, those who have committed the crimes, that the Prosecutor knows very well, is not here as an accused. So in summary, because there are many, I would like to say that I don't feel it up to the situation to testify because it seems to me invalid, useless, unjust, very unjust, to testify. I may say -- you can urge me to testify all day, but I cannot. Much as I wish to say something, much as I wish to testify, it's beyond me to do that. I have come here to have justice. I joined the war to defend my country and the things that occurred after the war have done us disgrace, I may say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. I realise we've gone, what, 17 minutes beyond the time we should have taken the break all because we have been having short breaks in between this morning, but just to make sure that we do not overstep the tapes, I will ask that we take a break now, maybe it will be a shorter one, can we come back at half past so that we start the next session at the time it's supposed to start. Take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mr. Kabashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Kabashi, you testified in the Limaj trial relating to the truthfulness of the statements that you made to the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you remember that? Your counsel just referred to it in court.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the counsel for everything he's done for me. And I thank the Court for its understanding. There is nothing more I can add to this trial. It's beyond me, it's impossible. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, are you prepared to answer any further questions in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: If I could, I would willingly do; but I cannot. I really cannot. I don't see any reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Can I ask you this, to clarify the -- is it your position relating to what you said in the trial in Limaj: Is what you said in that trial true?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: As I already stated, I am unable to discuss this issue further nor to answer more than I have done so far. What I said before this Court I accept, to my recollection; there are things that I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: When you said just a moment ago "what I said before this Court," do you mean this Chamber or both this Chamber and the last Chamber, the Limaj Chamber?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I don't know if you understand me, but there is nothing more I can add.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, if I show you your prior witness statements and as you to go through them, will that help you to remember any of the events or to help you to want to testify. In other words, if I show you those and go through them, will you answer my questions about them?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I already stated, it's not that I'm unwilling to reply to your questions; but I am unable to answer to any other question and I cannot provide any more assistance to this Chamber. It's inside me. You can do whatever you want me, you can kill me, you can imprison me, but I cannot. Maybe I'm a person who is not very clever. I haven't done a lot of schooling. Even my mother doesn't understand me properly, so I don't think you will either. But I would kindly ask you to let me go and you know why. I tried to explain even earlier. I hope it suffices. I don't know why you are -- I said even in the first session: Please, don't push me to say bad words which you can use against me then. You don't need to do that. If this trial is here to do justice, to discover crimes, and the Prosecutor's office has done nothing, then why do you involve me? I am a very insignificant player. It won't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, do you understand that this Trial Chamber wishes to hear your evidence about the matters that you saw and heard in 1998 in Jabllanice? Whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I said I am unable to speak about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you spoke about them in the past in the Limaj case. Why are you not able to speak about them again now?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: If you were in my shoes, you'd know why. Since you are not, you will never be able to understand the reason why. If you had passed through what I have -- you haven't gone halfway, I think, what I have done. I have suffered a lot and the burden is so heavy that I cannot lift myself up. I don't want you to urge me more than you are. Maybe I would even forget everything I have passed. If it's possible, that would be the best approach you would follow. But if you -- even if you accuse me of something, then I will let it to God to decide. My children have bread to eat. I grew up an orphan myself because he died very younger, younger than I am today, but he is three days -- three sons, sorry, they have survived and mine will survive. I leave it in the hands of God.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you have given a number of reasons why you don't wish to answer further questions. Earlier, His Honour was asking you about whether there was anything about which you were afraid and whether that was affecting you in any way from wishing to testify. Is there anything about that, about your -- are there any fears that you have for your own safety or the safety of anybody else should you continue to testify?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [In English] Do I look like one who is afraid?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just answer my question without posing a question.

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you have any -- I'll break it into two, see if you can answer this: Do you have any fears specifically for yourself, for your own safety or otherwise, should you answer questions?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I already answered the question to my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Do you have any fears for the safety of any other person should you answer questions?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I already stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, it would be of great assistance for us to be very clear on these two points, and I say you've stated it. Would you just state one more time for the record so it's very clear, whether you -- it can be yes or no, whether you have any fears for yourself if you were to continue to testify. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm not sure it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm quite sure it's clear if you take a look at the record, and really what is going on here is Mr. Rogers is using this as a device to seek to do something in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, it's most definitely right, and you know you are going to try to do it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It's a proper question in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In these circumstances this gentleman has repeatedly made himself clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In my entire experience of litigation, I have never seen a witness make himself clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: If Your Honours consider the matter is clear, then I need not pursue it; if Your Honours do not, then perhaps it would be best if it was abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, putting an adjective on the issue of clarity doesn't assist this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. The objection has been made. It's a matter for Your Honours to rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: The objection's overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, would you answer the question. Yes or no, are you afraid for yourself should you continue to testify in this matter?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: No, I am not afraid. But I am unable to testify. It's not a matter of fear. It's something that is inside me, a feeling I have inside myself, something that keeps you alive or makes you go on living in the place you live. There are many things there that prevent me. I'm trying, I'm doing my best, but I can't. I don't see any rights somewhere, prevailing somewhere, to give me a reason why. That's why I'm not testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: For the clarity, is there any reason as any fear that you have for the safety of any other person should you continue to testify?

utterances.speaker: SHEFQET KABASHI
utterances.text: I said what I wanted to say. I don't think I can say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have asked a direct question and asked for a yes or no answer. I wonder if you would direct the witness, please, to answer the question: Is he afraid for any other person should he continue to testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, are you -- will you please answer the question. Just say yes or no, whatever the answer is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't know whether you fear for somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There you are, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, this is as far as we can go on that particular issue. Would Your Honours bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, whilst Mr. Rogers is consulting, can I ask the record to note that on page 71, lines 21 to 23, when the witness is asked the question that he has just been asked immediately before his answer he was shaking his head which should appear on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 71, line ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: 21 to 23, the witness shook his head whilst giving his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: He did. I accept that. There may be all sorts of reasons for that, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, yes, to the extent that the video recording is of assistance to the Chamber in determining issues with regard to demeanour and credibility, I think that Mr. Emmerson's point is well taken and is something that should be in the Chamber's mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we've come to a stage where I have to consider what the further steps I should take in relation to seeking to continue to hear the evidence of this witness one way or another. I don't want to make a precipitate application. I'd rather consider it with care as to the next steps. I've tried memory-refreshing. The witness has not gone along that road. The next step is one I would like to consider, but I don't wish to discuss that in the presence of the witness. So as we come, I think, really to the end of this morning's proceedings or near to that, as far as we're able to go this morning, Your Honour, I wonder if the witness could leave for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Kabashi, you are excused for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if Mr. Rogers is going to outline the way in which his mind is working, we probably ought to be in private session. It would certainly help us to know what he intends to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to go into private session. I was going to outline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to outline it now or did you want to consider it? I thought you wanted to [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: No, I'll consider it, but I'm not going to make the application right this minute. I just wanted to tell Your Honours so that my learned friends are aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We are going to take an adjournment and we will come here tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, and Mr. Rogers will tell us then what his decision is. May the Chamber rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of August, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.10 p.m.,
